title: AIP-C01 Task 1.6 Exam Notes: Prompt Engineering and Governance
html:
AIP-C01 Task 1.6 Exam Notes: Prompt Engineering and Governance

How exam questions on Task 1.6 are worded, which answer wins, and why the others lose. Plus a recap of Domain 1. Task 1.6, post 7 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-6-exam.png — alt: "Task 1.6 exam notes"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.6: Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions · Post 7 of 7. Exam notes for the whole task, plus a recap of Domain 1.

The six previous posts explained each skill in Task 1.6. This one is for exam preparation: how questions on this task are worded, which answer wins, and why the other options lose. It's also the last post of Domain 1, so it ends with the whole domain on one page.

Task 1.6 on one page

Task 1.6: Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions has six skills. Here's the core idea of each, and the words in a question that should make you think of it:

[IMAGE: t1-6-summary.png — alt: "Task 1.6 summary: core idea and trigger words for skills 1.6.1 to 1.6.6"]

How to read a Task 1.6 question

  1. Is it a rule that must always hold? Then the answer is enforced outside the model: a guardrail, code, a workflow. Prompt wording alone loses.
  2. Is it about change over time? Versions, approval, pinned ARNs, CloudTrail and test suites. Editing a live prompt or draft loses.
  3. Is it about quality? Prompt techniques first (structure, format, chain of thought, feedback), measured on a labelled set. Fine-tuning comes after.

Skill 1.6.1: Instruction frameworks

[IMAGE: t1-6-1-exam.png — alt: "Exam scenarios for instruction frameworks: Prompt Management, denied topics, PII masking, prompt attack filter, ApplyGuardrail, response format"]

Traps: copying the system prompt into each application; “never discuss X” in the prompt instead of a denied topic; assuming guardrails only work with Bedrock models (ApplyGuardrail works on any text).

Covered in post 1: Skill 1.6.1: Control Model Behaviour with Prompt Management and Guardrails (lab).

Skill 1.6.2: Context in conversations

[IMAGE: t1-6-2-exam.png — alt: "Exam scenarios for conversation context: DynamoDB with TTL, sending history, summarising, Comprehend classification and sentiment, task tokens"]

Traps: expecting the model to remember earlier turns; a bigger context window instead of summarising; a large model to classify every message when Comprehend would do; polling for a user's reply instead of a task token.

Covered in post 2: Skill 1.6.2: Keep Context in Conversations.

Skill 1.6.3: Governance

[IMAGE: t1-6-3-exam.png — alt: "Exam scenarios for prompt governance: pin previous version, approval workflow, versioned S3 or Git, CloudTrail, invocation logging"]

Traps: fixing a bad change by re-editing the draft; looking for prompt content in CloudTrail; letting authors publish their own changes.

Covered in post 3: Skill 1.6.3: Govern Prompts with Versions, Approval and Audit (lab).

Skill 1.6.4: Prompt QA

[IMAGE: t1-6-4-exam.png — alt: "Exam scenarios for prompt QA: Lambda verification, Step Functions Map, CloudWatch metric and alarm, pass-rate gate, rerun after model upgrade"]

Traps: manual review of outputs; monitoring after release instead of gating before it; skipping the suite because “only the model version changed”.

Covered in post 4: Skill 1.6.4: Test Prompts Like Code (lab).

Skill 1.6.5: Iterative refinement

[IMAGE: t1-6-5-exam.png — alt: "Exam scenarios for prompt refinement: structured input, output format, chain of thought, feedback loop, labelled test set, fine-tuning last"]

Traps: raising temperature to fix reasoning; retrying until the output happens to parse; judging a change by a few demos; fine-tuning before prompt techniques are exhausted.

Covered in post 5: Skill 1.6.5: Improve Prompts Step by Step (lab).

Skill 1.6.6: Prompt chains

[IMAGE: t1-6-6-exam.png — alt: "Exam scenarios for prompt chains: Bedrock Flows, condition node, prompt nodes from Prompt Management, Lambda pre-processing, versions and alias, agent versus flow"]

Traps: one giant prompt for every intent; routing code in Lambda when a condition node does it; editing a live flow; a flow when the model must choose its own steps (that's an agent).

Covered in post 6: Skill 1.6.6: Chain Prompts with Bedrock Flows (lab).

Keyword shortcuts for Task 1.6

  • “Same role and rules across applications” → Bedrock Prompt Management
  • “Never discuss a topic” → guardrail denied topic
  • “Mask PII” → guardrail sensitive information filter (anonymize)
  • “Jailbreak, ignore your instructions” → guardrail prompt attack filter
  • “Same safety policy for another model or any text” → ApplyGuardrail
  • “Conversation history by session” → DynamoDB with TTL
  • “Recognise intent, detect frustration” → Amazon Comprehend
  • “Ask for missing details, then continue” → Step Functions task token
  • “Roll back a prompt” → pin the previous version ARN
  • “Who changed the prompt” → CloudTrail; “what the model received” → model invocation logging
  • “Detect prompt regression” → test suite + CloudWatch pass-rate metric and alarm
  • “Inconsistent format, reasoning errors” → output specification, chain of thought, feedback loop
  • “Classify, then branch to different prompts” → Bedrock Flows with a condition node

Domain 1 on one page

That completes all six tasks and 28 skills of Domain 1: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance, 31% of the exam. Here's the whole domain, with the services that come up most:

[IMAGE: d1-recap.png — alt: "Domain 1 on one page: tasks 1.1 to 1.6, what each covers and the services that appear most"]

Before moving on, reread the exam notes post for each task (1.1 to 1.6) in one sitting. The same habits run through the whole domain: pick the managed option when it fits, put rules that must hold outside the model, measure before and after every change, and keep everything versioned so it can be rolled back.

Practice questions

Practice questions for Task 1.6 and the rest of Domain 1 will be added in a later post. Until then, the official AWS Skill Builder practice question set is the closest thing to the real exam.
